## Historical thinking

Historical thinking asks us to consider why we examine the past in order to better understand the world around us and the world ahead of us. In EDUC 219, historical inquiry helps us become better informed citizens and education professionals by connecting evidence, institutions, events, and ideas to questions about schooling, democracy, access, diversity, and social justice.

## Your group’s work

You will work individually and collaboratively to:

-   Define criteria for identifying major historical events.
-   Select two historical bookend events within a broader historical period.
-   Identify and document two primary-source artifacts situated between those events.
-   Create a physical historical timeline with a group.
-   Contribute records to the class digital timeline/database.
-   Identify whether timeline entries are classified as major events and whether they are directly related to education.

[Add data to the database](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1yUIsKRk3E0qLV6HYIF8q36WobMfrU2W7VqieMk2soT4/edit?usp=sharing){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

## Class timeline roles

As we create the shared digital timeline, students may contribute through one of three roles:

-   **Transcribers:** Integrate physical timelines into the class Excel database; document events and artifacts; and help scale or weight major and non-major events.
-   **Coders:** Use the shared database to help generate a digital timeline. No software downloads are required.
-   **Translators:** Work across the transcription and coding groups to identify, categorize, and highlight education-related events, sources, and themes.

::: callout-note

## Connection to the trials

The timeline and database will provide a shared historical resource for the course.

Your group’s research may connect directly to *Plessy v. Ferguson*, *Brown v. Board of Education*, both cases, or broader historical periods that help us understand the social, political, legal, and educational contexts surrounding the trials.

Use your archival work to identify evidence, historical context, educational themes, and questions that can strengthen your trial-group research and reenactment preparation.
